item.title: Siromi Turaga has resigned as Acting Attorney General
item.description: Mikaele Liga , Vijay Narayan · 13/10/2026 Siromi Turaga has resigned as Acting Attorney General.
item.content:encoded:
Mikaele Liga , Vijay Narayan · 13/10/2026

Siromi Turaga has resigned as Acting Attorney General.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka confirmed this to the media earlier this afternoon.

Rabuka says Turaga is still a Member of Parliament and People's Alliance Party member.

He says his resignation is effective immediately.

The Prime Minister says Turaga is still involved in the People's Alliance Party discussions and the Special Committee.

He says he told Turaga that he believes there is a video that is being circulated.

Rabuka says Turaga came up with an apology and offered to resign from cabinet.

The Prime Minister says as of now, they have not seen or appointed anyone to replace Turaga.

Rabuka says they have a team in cabinet that is already legally qualified but not constitutionally qualified.

item.title: Human Rights Commission calls for extension of Constitution Bill submissions
item.description: The Fiji Human Rights and Anti-Discrimination Commission is calling on Parliament to extend the 11-day public submission period for the Constitution Amendment Bill 2026, warning that the timeframe limits meaningful public participation in a process that will shape Fiji’s democratic future. Commissioner Alefina Vuki says the public needs adequate time and accessible information to understand the pr
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Human Rights and Anti-Discrimination Commission is calling on Parliament to extend the 11-day public submission period for the Constitution Amendment Bill 2026, warning that the timeframe limits meaningful public participation in a process that will shape Fiji’s democratic future.

Commissioner Alefina Vuki says the public needs adequate time and accessible information to understand the proposed amendments and their implications before providing feedback.

The Special Committee reviewing the Bill issued a notice yesterday, setting October 23rd as the deadline for written submissions.

Vuki says this timeframe leaves less than two working weeks for individuals, communities and organisations to examine the proposed changes and prepare informed submissions.

She says the process is particularly challenging because the public would need to understand both the draft Constitution prepared by the Constitution Review Committee and the revised draft containing substantial changes made by the Government.

Vuki says meaningful consultation requires more than publishing a Bill and inviting submissions, as people must understand what is being proposed, why the changes are being sought and how they could affect them.

She says Fiji’s geographical circumstances also present challenges, with people in rural communities, remote villages and maritime islands facing varying levels of access to information, transport and internet connectivity.

She says they are also calling for measures to ensure vulnerable and marginalised groups, including people with disabilities, older persons, women, young people and people living in poverty, can participate in the consultation process.

Vuki says this requires accessible information, translations into relevant languages, reasonable accommodation and proactive community engagement.

The Commission has also raised concerns about the proposed national referendum, saying voters need sufficient time and impartial information to understand the process, the choices they will be asked to make and the consequences of their decisions.

She says comprehensive civic education is necessary to ensure the referendum is an informed exercise rather than simply a voting process.

They also note that Fiji, as a State Party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, has obligations under Article 25 to protect citizens’ rights and opportunities to participate in public affairs without unreasonable restrictions.

They argue that limiting submissions to 11 days while moving towards a proposed referendum on December 9th this year risks undermining that right.

item.title: Naivalurua reviewing suspected cyber attack on Suva-based regional organisation
item.description: Rashika Kumar , Mikaele Liga · 13/10/2026 Minister for Policing and Communications Ioane Naivalurua says they are reviewing the situation where the US Embassy has informed the Fijian Government of a suspected cyber attack on a regional organisation based in Suva.
item.content:encoded:
Rashika Kumar , Mikaele Liga · 13/10/2026

Minister for Policing and Communications Ioane Naivalurua says they are reviewing the situation where the US Embassy has informed the Fijian Government of a suspected cyber attack on a regional organisation based in Suva.

The Embassy says hackers linked to China believed to have accessed the organisation’s network for several days.

The say the suspected compromise occurred between July and August this year.

The Embassy says they have also provided technical recommendations to the Fijian Government and the affected organisation on steps they could take to protect their networks and strengthen cybersecurity.

While responding to fijivillage News, the Embassy says they cannot provide further details or disclose the name of the organisation affected by this recent cyber incident. They say the purpose of this disclosure is to highlight a trend the United States continues to observe across Pacific Islands countries of state-sponsored cyber threat actors linked to China targeting foreign governments, multilateral organizations, and telecommunications networks.

Meanwhile, the Embassy confirms the United States Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation seized platforms “QScan” and “QTRouter,” operated and used by China state-sponsored hackers to target critical infrastructure in the United States.

The Embassy says the Department and FBI takedown matters directly for the Pacific.

They say China's state-sponsored malicious hackers try to hide their tracks while targeting critical infrastructure, not just in the United States, but around the world, including right here in Pacific.

They say there are several news reports on this troubling trend in the Pacific over the past few years.

The Chinese Embassy in Fiji says cybersecurity is an issue of common concern for China and the U.S.

They are urging the U.S. to quit double standards and political manipulation, jointly tackle cybersecurity risks through equal-footed dialogue and build a relationship characterized by peace, stability and mutual respect on cyber issues.

Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning says China and the U.S. should jointly address the risks of cyber security and build a peaceful, stable, and mutually respectful Sino-U.S network relationship.

Naivalurua is expected to provide a further response soon.

Questions have also been sent to the Minister for Foreign Affairs Sakiasi Ditoka on whether concerns are being raised with the Chinese Embassy.

item.title: Fiji Airways brings about 70% of visitors to Fiji – Patel
item.description: Fiji Airways carries about 70 percent of all visitors arriving in Fiji, making it one of the major contributors to the country's economy, particularly the tourism and trade sectors. Fiji Airways Board Chairman Nalin Patel highlighted this while making submissions on the airline's 2024 Annual Report to the Standing Committee on Social Affairs.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji Airways carries about 70 percent of all visitors arriving in Fiji, making it one of the major contributors to the country's economy, particularly the tourism and trade sectors.

Fiji Airways Board Chairman Nalin Patel highlighted this while making submissions on the airline's 2024 Annual Report to the Standing Committee on Social Affairs.

Patel says the airline plays a significant role in connecting Fiji to the rest of the world and supporting the country's tourism industry.

He says Fiji Airways operates approximately 23 aircraft, most of which are modern, providing around three million passenger seats.

However, Patel says the challenge is to turn this available capacity into more visitors travelling to Fiji and staying in the country rather than simply transiting through.

He also highlighted accommodation capacity as a challenge in encouraging transit passengers to stay in Fiji.

Patel says Fiji Airways currently serves 36 international destinations and has strengthened its global connectivity through its full membership in the Oneworld, alongside major international airlines such as Qantas, British Airways, Japan Airlines and Qatar Airways.

He says the partnership provides opportunities for Fiji Airways to work with larger airlines, improve its services and strengthen international connections.

item.title: Tovata water outage disrupts school and Navratri preparations as WAF carries out repairs
item.description: Families in Tovata, Makoi, are struggling without water following a burst water main, with some students missing school and residents facing difficulties preparing for Navratri celebrations, as the Water Authority of Fiji carries out repairs. A resident says the disruption has been particularly challenging for families observing Navratri, as water is needed for household prayers, preparing food, a
item.content:encoded:
Families in Tovata, Makoi, are struggling without water following a burst water main, with some students missing school and residents facing difficulties preparing for Navratri celebrations, as the Water Authority of Fiji carries out repairs.

A resident says the disruption has been particularly challenging for families observing Navratri, as water is needed for household prayers, preparing food, and hosting visitors.

The resident says students have also been affected, with some unable to attend school due to the lack of water, while a funeral in the community has added to the challenges faced by families.

They say the water supply was still disrupted after they first noticed the issue early in the morning and are concerned about recurring water cuts in the area.

The resident says they contacted the Water Authority of Fiji at around 8.30am and were told other residents had been calling since 6am to report the issue.

They say they called again at around 9.30am but were informed that WAF was still trying to establish the cause of the disruption.

The resident claims several water pipes had burst along the road, which they believe caused the interruption to the supply.

They say the customer care line remained busy until around midday, when a representative informed them that a WAF team would attend to the matter, with water expected to be restored by 4pm.

The resident says this is not the first time residents have experienced water disruptions , saying burst pipes and leakages have occurred repeatedly in the area.

They are calling for water pipes to be installed at a lower level where possible and for regular checks to identify and repair leakages before they cause widespread disruptions.

The resident says unexpected water cuts make it difficult for people to manage their daily responsibilities and is calling for a more reliable water supply and timely communication from WAF.

Meanwhile, WAF has confirmed that a burst water main line has disrupted supply to Tovata, Makoi and Kalabu.

WAF says the disruption was scheduled from 10.30am to 3pm, with repairs and maintenance expected to be completed by 3.30pm, followed by gradual restoration of water supply.

item.title: New digital hub helps Fiji election candidates plan campaigns and calculate vote targets
item.description: Prospective election candidates in Fiji can now calculate vote targets, develop campaign strategies and budgets, prepare nomination documents and assess safety risks through a new digital platform launched by the Centre for Democracy & Dialogue (CDD). The Empowering Fiji’s Women in Politics Candidate Hub was officially launched today by Supervisor of Elections Ana Mataiciwa, bringing together elec
item.content:encoded:
Prospective election candidates in Fiji can now calculate vote targets, develop campaign strategies and budgets, prepare nomination documents and assess safety risks through a new digital platform launched by the Centre for Democracy & Dialogue (CDD).

The Empowering Fiji’s Women in Politics Candidate Hub was officially launched today by Supervisor of Elections Ana Mataiciwa, bringing together electoral education, campaign planning, mentoring and nine interactive tools designed for Fiji’s electoral environment.

CDD Chief Executive Officer Nilesh Lal says the platform is designed to help candidates move beyond general campaign plans and develop practical strategies based on the votes they need, available resources and time.

Lal says candidates can use the tools to assess their readiness, identify priority voter groups, estimate the number of people they need to reach and determine whether their campaign budgets and volunteer resources are sufficient.

The platform includes six learning modules covering Fiji’s political and electoral systems, candidate eligibility, media and communications, campaign finance and legal compliance, leadership, policy and public service.

Its nine interactive tools include a Personal Vote Target Calculator, Campaign Strategy Builder, Campaign Budget Builder, Candidate Readiness Assessment, Election Timeline Calculator, Candidate Eligibility Self-Check, Nomination Readiness Checklist, Campaign Message Builder and Women Candidate Safety Planner.

The Campaign Budget Builder allows candidates to identify funding and expenditure, assess cash flow, distinguish essential from optional spending and prepare campaign compliance records.

The Women Candidate Safety Planner helps users assess risks associated with physical safety, travel, online harassment, reputational attacks, public events and wellbeing. CDD says sensitive planning information in key tools remains in the user's browser rather than being stored by the organisation.

Although developed under CDD's programme to empower women in politics, the platform is publicly available to all prospective candidates and campaign teams.

Lal says the initiative aims to increase women's participation and electoral success while helping candidates across the political spectrum make better-informed decisions and comply with electoral laws.

Meanwhile, CDD also launched a 20-page toolkit titled AI & Your Campaign , which addresses the growing use of artificial intelligence in elections.

The Fiji-specific resource explains how candidates can identify and respond to deepfake videos and images, voice cloning, fabricated news sites, bot networks, false voter information and gender-based AI attacks.

It also outlines the SIFT verification method, provides a rapid-response framework for AI-related attacks and explains relevant reporting pathways and laws in Fiji.

The toolkit encourages candidates to use artificial intelligence responsibly for activities such as drafting campaign materials, analysing information, translation and multilingual communication.

Lal says candidates need to prepare for AI-related threats before manipulated content spreads among voters.

CDD is inviting registered political parties, prospective candidates and campaign teams to access the resources and seek demonstrations, technical briefings and training.

The Candidate Hub is available at cdd.org.fj/efwip-candidate-hub, while the AI toolkit can be accessed through CDD's publications portal.

item.title: Save the Children Fiji calls for removal of ‘lawful and moderate chastisement’ clause in the proposed Constitution
item.description: The organisation says the proposed exception in the Constitution (Amendment) Bill 2026 is open to interpretation and could be used to justify physical punishment or other harmful behaviour towards children. Under the proposed amendment, children would continue to have the right to protection from abuse, neglect, harmful cultural practices, violence and inhumane treatment and punishment.
item.content:encoded:
The organisation says the proposed exception in the Constitution (Amendment) Bill 2026 is open to interpretation and could be used to justify physical punishment or other harmful behaviour towards children.

Under the proposed amendment, children would continue to have the right to protection from abuse, neglect, harmful cultural practices, violence and inhumane treatment and punishment.

However, the Bill would add an exception allowing “lawful and moderate chastisement for the purposes of correction.”

Save the Children Fiji Program Manager John Bryan Mausio says Fiji’s Constitution should provide children with clear and unequivocal protection from all forms of violence.

Mausio says the proposed provision sends the wrong message at a time when Fiji should be strengthening efforts to prevent violence against children and promote positive, non-violent approaches to parenting and discipline.

Mausio says the phrase “lawful and moderate chastisement” is open to interpretation and could create uncertainty over what conduct is considered acceptable.

He says there is a risk the exception could be used to justify harmful behaviour towards children.

He says there should be zero tolerance for violence against children, regardless of the intention behind it.

The organisation says the debate should not be framed as a choice between discipline and no discipline, but should focus on positive discipline approaches that teach responsibility, accountability and respect without violence, humiliation or fear.

It says positive discipline includes setting clear expectations and boundaries, using age-appropriate consequences, encouraging positive behaviour and helping children understand the impact of their actions.

The organisation also cites World Health Organization research which has found that corporal punishment can harm children’s physical and mental health, increase behavioural problems and carries a risk of escalating into more serious violence.

Mausio says Fiji has made important progress in strengthening child protection and promoting children’s rights, and any constitutional amendment should reinforce rather than dilute those protections.

He says Fiji ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1993 and has since made commitments to invest in the welfare and protection of children.

Mausio says the proposed amendment contradicts those commitments and could compromise the effectiveness of child protection systems, including the national child helpline.

He says it has worked with the Government, including the Ministry of Women, Children and Social Protection and the Ministry of Education, to strengthen national efforts to prevent violence, harm and abuse against children.

The organisation maintains that the provision permitting “lawful and moderate chastisement” must be removed and that the Constitution should provide children with consistent protection from all forms of violence.
